items.statement: Let there be ν subsets of R^l, 𝔄_ι (ι = 1, …, ν). Let 𝔄 = 𝔄_1 × 𝔄_2 × … × 𝔄_ν, i.e., 𝔄 is the set of ordered ν-tuples a = (a_1, …, a_ν) where a_ι ∈ 𝔄_ι for ι = 1, …, ν. For each ι, suppose there is a real function f_ι defined over 𝔄. Let ā_ι = (a_1, …, a_{ι−1}, a_{ι+1}, …, a_ν) ∈ 𝔄̄_ι = 𝔄_1 × … × 𝔄_{ι−1} × 𝔄_{ι+1} × … × 𝔄_ν. Let A_ι(ā_ι) be a function defining for each point ā_ι ∈ 𝔄̄_ι a subset of 𝔄_ι. Then the sequence [𝔄_1, …, 𝔄_ν, f_1, …, f_ν, A_1(ā_1), …, A_ν(ā_ν)] is termed an abstract economy.
items.context: Introduces the abstract economy as a generalization of a game where each participant's feasible action set may depend on the actions of others.

notation_in_scope.𝔄_ι: action set for participant ι, a subset of R^l
notation_in_scope.𝔄: product of all action sets 𝔄_1 × … × 𝔄_ν
notation_in_scope.f_ι: payoff function for participant ι, defined on 𝔄
notation_in_scope.ā_ι: actions of all participants except ι
notation_in_scope.𝔄̄_ι: product of action sets of all participants except ι
notation_in_scope.A_ι(ā_ι): feasible action set for ι given others' actions ā_ι

items.statement: If the functions A_ι(ā_ι) are constants, i.e., A_ι(ā_ι) is a fixed subset of 𝔄_ι independent of ā_ι (in particular, if A_ι(ā_ι) = 𝔄_ι for all ι), then the abstract economy [𝔄_1, …, 𝔄_ν, f_1, …, f_ν, A_1(ā_1), …, A_ν(ā_ν)] reduces to a game.
items.proof_sketch: When A_ι is constant, each player's strategy domain is independent of others' choices, matching the standard game-theoretic setup.
items.context: The text establishes that a game is a special case of an abstract economy where feasible sets do not depend on other agents' actions.

notation_in_scope.A_ι(ā_ι): feasible action set, here assumed constant

items.statement: An abstract economy is a generalization of a game in which the choice of an action by one agent affects both the payoff and the domain of actions of other agents.
items.context: In a game, only payoffs depend on others' strategies; in an abstract economy, feasible sets also depend on others' actions. The need for this generalization arises from the consumer's budget constraint depending on prices and income determined by other agents.

items.statement: Nash (1950) formally introduced the notion of an equilibrium point for a game. The concept had been formulated by Cournot in the special case of an oligopolistic economy.
items.context: Referenced as Nash [14] and Cournot [3]. The equilibrium concept is extended from games to abstract economies.

items.statement: The Theorem in Debreu [5] (A Social Equilibrium Existence Theorem, 1952), which establishes existence of equilibrium for generalized games using contractible polyhedra and fixed point methods, together with the Remark on p. 889 of that paper.
items.context: Debreu [5], pp. 888-889. Lemma 2.5 is a special case of this theorem.

items.statement: a* is an equilibrium point of [𝔄_1, …, 𝔄_ν, f_1, …, f_ν, A_1(ā_1), …, A_ν(ā_ν)] if, for all ι = 1, …, ν: (1) a*_ι ∈ A_ι(ā*_ι), and (2) f_ι(a*_ι, ā*_ι) = max_{a_ι ∈ A_ι(ā*_ι)} f_ι(a_ι, ā*_ι).
items.context: Formally labeled DEFINITION. Extends Nash's equilibrium concept to abstract economies. Each individual maximizes their payoff over the set of actions permitted by the other agents' actions.

notation_in_scope.ā*_ι: equilibrium actions of all participants except ι
notation_in_scope.A_ι(ā*_ι): feasible set for ι at equilibrium

items.statement: The graph of A_ι(ā_ι) is the set { a | a_ι ∈ A_ι(ā_ι) }, i.e., the set of all action profiles a ∈ 𝔄 such that ι's component a_ι belongs to the feasible set A_ι(ā_ι) determined by the other components. This generalizes to the multi-valued functions A_ι(ā_ι) the ordinary definition of the graph of a function.
items.context: Repeated from Debreu [5], pp. 888-889.

items.statement: The function A_ι(ā_ι) is said to be continuous at ā⁰_ι if for every a⁰_ι ∈ A_ι(ā⁰_ι) and every sequence {ā^n_ι} converging to ā⁰_ι, there is a sequence {a^n_ι} converging to a⁰_ι such that a^n_ι ∈ A_ι(ā^n_ι) for all n.
items.context: Repeated from Debreu [5]. If A_ι were single-valued, this definition coincides with the ordinary definition of continuity.

items.statement: If, for each ι: (1) 𝔄_ι is compact and convex, (2) f_ι(a_ι, ā_ι) is continuous on 𝔄 and quasi-concave in a_ι for every ā_ι, (3) A_ι(ā_ι) is a continuous function whose graph is a closed set, and (4) for every ā_ι, the set A_ι(ā_ι) is convex and non-empty, then the abstract economy [𝔄_1, …, 𝔄_ν, f_1, …, f_ν, A_1(ā_1), …, A_ν(ā_ν)] has an equilibrium point.
items.proof_sketch: This is a special case of the Theorem in Debreu [5], when taken in conjunction with the Remark on p. 889. A compact convex set is a contractible polyhedron; compactness of the graph of A_ι follows from its closure and the compactness of 𝔄; the set of optimal actions for ι given ā_ι is convex (hence contractible) when f_ι is quasi-concave in a_ι.
items.context: Formally labeled LEMMA. Central to all existence proofs in the paper. Generalizes Nash's theorem on equilibrium points for games to abstract economies.

items.statement: Lemma 2.5 generalizes Nash's theorem on the existence of equilibrium points for games.
items.proof_sketch: A game is the special case where A_ι(ā_ι) = 𝔄_ι (constant). In that case the continuity and closure conditions on A_ι are trivially satisfied.

items.statement: A compact convex set is necessarily a contractible polyhedron.
items.context: Stated in footnote 10, used to verify that the conditions of Debreu [5] are met by Lemma 2.5's hypotheses.

items.statement: If the graph of A_ι(ā_ι) is a closed set and 𝔄 (which contains the graph) is compact, then the graph of A_ι(ā_ι) is compact.
items.proof_sketch: A closed subset of a compact set is compact.
items.context: Stated in footnote 10, bridging the conditions of Lemma 2.5 to those of Debreu [5].

items.statement: For any given ā_ι, the set { a_ι | a_ι ∈ A_ι(ā_ι), f_ι(a_ι, ā_ι) = max_{a'_ι ∈ A_ι(ā_ι)} f_ι(a'_ι, ā_ι) } is a convex set when f_ι(a_ι, ā_ι) is quasi-concave in a_ι.
items.proof_sketch: The set of maximizers of a quasi-concave function over a convex set is convex.
items.context: Stated in footnote 10. This convexity ensures the set is contractible, as required by Debreu [5].

items.statement: Define an abstract economy E with m + n + 1 participants as follows. There are m consumption units with action sets X_i, n production units with action sets Y_j, and one market participant with action set P. For consumption unit i, let x̄_i denote a point in X_1 × … × X_{i−1} × X_{i+1} × … × X_m × Y_1 × … × Y_n × P. Define A_i(x̄_i) = { x_i | x_i ∈ X_i, p·x_i ≤ p·ω_i + max[0, Σ_{j=1}^n α_{ij} p·y_j] }. The abstract economy is E = [X_1, …, X_m, Y_1, …, Y_n, P, u_1(x_1), …, u_m(x_m), p·y_1, …, p·y_n, p·z, A_1(x̄_1), …, A_m(x̄_m), Y_1, …, Y_n, P], where: consumption unit i chooses x_i from X_i subject to x_i ∈ A_i(x̄_i) with payoff u_i(x_i); production unit j chooses y_j from Y_j (unrestricted) with payoff p·y_j; the market participant chooses p from P (unrestricted) with payoff p·z, where z = Σ_i x_i − Σ_j y_j − ω.
items.context: This defines the specific abstract economy whose equilibrium points will be shown to be competitive equilibria. The domains X_i, Y_j, P are defined in 1.3.0, 1.2.2, 1.4.0 respectively.

notation_in_scope.z: excess demand vector z = Σ_i x_i − Σ_j y_j − ω
notation_in_scope.α_{ij}: share of consumer i in firm j's profit

items.statement: For the market participant with payoff p·z, taking z as given, the payoff p·z is a linear function of p. It can be increased by increasing p_h for commodities with z_h > 0 and decreasing p_h if z_h < 0 (provided p_h > 0). This adjustment rule is precisely the classical law of supply and demand.
items.proof_sketch: p·z = Σ_h p_h z_h is linear in p. The gradient with respect to p is z, so increasing p_h when z_h > 0 increases the payoff.
items.context: Motivates the market participant's payoff function as encoding Walrasian price adjustment.

items.statement: In the definition of A_i(x̄_i), the expression Σ_{j=1}^n α_{ij} p·y_j is replaced by max[0, Σ_{j=1}^n α_{ij} p·y_j]. This ensures A_i(x̄_i) is non-empty: since by Assumption IV.a there exists x'_i ∈ X_i with ω_i ≥ x'_i, we have p·ω_i ≥ p·x'_i, and therefore p·x'_i ≤ p·ω_i ≤ p·ω_i + max[0, Σ_j α_{ij} p·y_j], so x'_i ∈ A_i(x̄_i).
items.proof_sketch: By Assumption IV.a, ω_i ≥ x'_i for some x'_i ∈ X_i. Since p ≥ 0, p·ω_i ≥ p·x'_i. Adding the non-negative max term to the right-hand side preserves the inequality.
items.context: The max[0, …] replacement is needed because for arbitrary choices of p and y_j, the original budget set might be empty.

items.statement: At an equilibrium point of E (denoted by asterisks), p*·y*_j ≥ 0 for each j.
items.proof_sketch: By the definition of E-equilibrium, y*_j maximizes p*·y_j subject to y_j ∈ Y_j. By Assumption I.a, 0 ∈ Y_j. Hence p*·y*_j ≥ p*·0 = 0.
items.context: Equation (1) of 3.1.2. Follows from profit maximization and the fact that inaction (0) is always feasible for firms.

notation_in_scope.y*_j: equilibrium production vector for firm j

items.statement: At an equilibrium point of E, by Assumption IV.b (Σ_i α_{ij} = 1) and p*·y*_j ≥ 0, we have Σ_j α_{ij} p*·y*_j ≥ 0, so max[0, Σ_j α_{ij} p*·y*_j] = Σ_j α_{ij} p*·y*_j. Therefore at equilibrium, A_i(x̄*_i) = {x_i ∈ X_i : p*·x_i ≤ p*·ω_i + Σ_j α_{ij} p*·y*_j}, and the max[0, …] substitution makes no difference.
items.proof_sketch: Since p*·y*_j ≥ 0 and α_{ij} ≥ 0, each term α_{ij} p*·y*_j ≥ 0. The max operator becomes redundant, recovering the original budget constraint.
items.context: Shows the max[0, …] substitution makes no difference at equilibrium.

items.statement: Condition 2 (utility maximization subject to budget constraint) is satisfied at an equilibrium point of the abstract economy E.
items.proof_sketch: From Claim_3.1.2_c, at equilibrium the budget set coincides with the standard budget set. The equilibrium definition requires x*_i to maximize u_i(x_i) over A_i(x̄*_i), which is exactly Condition 2.
items.context: Labeled as equation (2) in section 3.1.2. First step in showing E-equilibrium implies competitive equilibrium.

items.statement: At an equilibrium point of E, Conditions 1 (profit maximization) and 3 (price in P) follow immediately from the definition of equilibrium point and the payoffs specified.
items.proof_sketch: Condition 1: y*_j maximizes p*·y_j for y_j ∈ Y_j by the equilibrium condition for production units. Condition 3: p* ∈ P by the equilibrium condition for the market participant's domain.

items.statement: At an equilibrium point of E, p*·z* = 0, where z* = Σ_i x*_i − Σ_j y*_j − ω is the excess demand vector.
items.proof: From Condition 2 (shown in Claim_3.1.2_d) and Assumptions III.b and III.c, the budget constraint holds with equality for each consumer (equation (1) of 1.4.2): p*·x*_i = p*·ω_i + Σ_j α_{ij} p*·y*_j. Summing over i and using Assumption IV.b (Σ_i α_{ij} = 1): p*·(Σ_i x*_i) = p*·ω + p*·(Σ_j y*_j), giving p*·z* = 0.
items.context: Equation (1) of section 3.2. Walras' Law: the value of excess demand is zero at equilibrium.

items.statement: At an equilibrium point of E, z*_h ≤ 0 for all h = 1, …, l.
items.proof: Let δ_h be the unit vector with 1 in component h and 0 elsewhere. Then δ_h ∈ P (by Condition 3, definition of P in 1.4.0). By the definition of equilibrium point, p* maximizes p·z* for p ∈ P. Hence 0 = p*·z* ≥ δ_h·z* = z*_h for all h.
items.context: Equation (2) of section 3.2. Market clearing in the weak sense: excess demand is non-positive for every commodity.

notation_in_scope.δ_h: unit vector of the hth axis in R^l
notation_in_scope.z*_h: excess demand for commodity h at equilibrium

items.statement: Any equilibrium point of E satisfies Conditions 1–4 and hence is a competitive equilibrium. Conversely, any competitive equilibrium is an equilibrium point of E.
items.proof_sketch: Condition 2 from Claim_3.1.2_d. Conditions 1 and 3 from Claim_3.2_a. Condition 4 (p*·z* = 0 and z* ≤ 0) from Claims 3.2_b and 3.2_c. The converse is obvious from the construction.
items.context: Establishes the equivalence between E-equilibrium and competitive equilibrium.

items.statement: X*_i = { x_i | x_i ∈ X_i, there exist x_{i'} ∈ X_{i'} for each i' ≠ i and y_j ∈ Y_j for each j such that z ≤ 0 }, where z = Σ_i x_i − Σ_j y_j − ω. X*_i is the set of consumption vectors available to individual i if he had complete control of the economy but had to take account of resource limitations.
items.context: Introduced because the Lemma of 2.5 is not directly applicable to E since the action spaces are not compact.

notation_in_scope.X*_i: set of feasible consumption vectors for i under resource constraints

items.statement: Y*_j = { y_j | y_j ∈ Y_j, there exist x_i ∈ X_i for each i and y_{j'} ∈ Y_{j'} for each j' ≠ j such that z ≤ 0 }. Y*_j is the set of production vectors available to firm j if it had complete control of the economy subject to resource limitations.
items.context: Y*_j has a similar interpretation to X*_i for production.

notation_in_scope.Y*_j: set of feasible production vectors for j under resource constraints

items.statement: An E-equilibrium x*_i must belong to X*_i, and an E-equilibrium y*_j must belong to Y*_j.
items.proof_sketch: At equilibrium, z* ≤ 0 (from Claim_3.2_c), so the equilibrium vectors satisfy the feasibility condition defining X*_i and Y*_j.
items.context: Justifies restricting attention to bounded sets without losing equilibria.

items.statement: Y*_j is bounded for all j.
items.proof: Suppose Y*_1 is unbounded. Then there exist sequences y^k_j ∈ Y_j and x^k_i ∈ X_i such that ||y^k_1|| → ∞ and Σ_j y^k_j − Σ_i x^k_i ≥ −ω. From Assumption II, Σ_i x^k_i ≥ Σ_i x̌_i for some lower bound, so Σ_j y^k_j is also unbounded. Let λ_k = max_j ||y^k_j||; for k sufficiently large, λ_k > 1. By convexity of Y_j (from Assumption I.a) and 0 ∈ Y_j, (1/λ_k)y^k_j ∈ Y_j. Passing to a convergent subsequence, (1/λ_{k_q})y^{k_q}_j → ŷ_j with Σ_j ŷ_j ≥ 0 and ŷ_j ∈ Y_j (by closure of Y_j). So ŷ = Σ_j ŷ_j ∈ Y (aggregate production set). By Assumption I.b (Y ∩ R^l_+ = {0}), ŷ = 0, implying ŷ_j = 0 for each j. But ||ŷ_j|| = lim (1/λ_{k_q})||y^{k_q}_j||, and for infinitely many q, max_j ||y^{k_q}_j|| = ||y^{k_q}_{j'}|| for some fixed j', giving ||ŷ_{j'}|| > 0, a contradiction.
items.context: Equation (7) in section 3.3.1. The boundedness of Y*_j is essential for compactifying the abstract economy.

notation_in_scope.Y*_j: feasible production set for firm j

items.statement: X*_i is bounded for all i.
items.proof: Let x_i ∈ X*_i. By definition, there exist x_{i'} ∈ X_{i'} and y_j ∈ Y_j such that z ≤ 0, i.e., Σ_{i'} x_{i'} ≤ Σ_j y_j + ω. It follows that y_j ∈ Y*_j for all j. Also x_i ≤ Σ_j y_j − Σ_{i' ≠ i} x_{i'} + ω. The right-hand side involves only elements of Y*_j (bounded by Claim_3.3.1) and elements of X_{i'} (bounded below by Assumption II). Hence the right-hand side is bounded above, and X*_i is bounded.
items.context: Equation (2) in section 3.3.2. Completes the boundedness argument needed for compactification.

items.statement: Choose a positive real number c so that the cube C = { x | |x_h| ≤ c for all h } contains in its interior all X*_i and all Y*_j. Let X̄_i = X_i ∩ C and Ȳ_j = Y_j ∩ C.
items.context: The bounded sets X̄_i and Ȳ_j will replace X_i and Y_j to obtain a compact economy.

notation_in_scope.C: cube { x | |x_h| ≤ c for all h }
notation_in_scope.c: chosen sufficiently large positive real number

items.statement: Define a new abstract economy Ē, identical with E in 3.1.0, except that X_i is replaced by X̄_i and Y_j by Ȳ_j everywhere. Let Ā_i(x̄_i) be the resultant modification of A_i(x̄_i), i.e., Ā_i(x̄_i) = A_i(x̄_i) ∩ C.
items.context: The truncated economy Ē has compact action sets, making the Lemma applicable.

items.statement: X̄_i and Ȳ_j are compact convex sets.
items.proof_sketch: From Assumptions II and I.a, X_i and Y_j are closed convex sets. C is a compact convex set. The intersection of a closed convex set with a compact convex set is compact and convex.
items.context: Verifies the first condition of Lemma 2.5 for the truncated economy Ē.

items.statement: P is compact and convex.
items.proof_sketch: P is the standard simplex in R^l, which is obviously compact and convex by its definition.
items.context: Verifies the compactness and convexity condition of Lemma 2.5 for the market participant's domain.

items.statement: For a consumption unit, the payoff u_i(x_i) is continuous and quasi-concave in x_i (by Assumptions III.a and III.c). For a production unit, the payoff p·y_j is continuous and quasi-concave (linear functions are quasi-concave). For the market participant, p·z is continuous and quasi-concave in p.
items.proof_sketch: Continuity and quasi-concavity of u_i follow from III.a and III.c. Linearity of p·y_j and p·z implies both continuity and quasi-concavity.
items.context: Verifies the second condition of Lemma 2.5 (payoff functions continuous and quasi-concave).

items.statement: For a production unit or the market participant, the feasible set (Ȳ_j or P) is a constant (independent of other agents' actions) and therefore trivially continuous with closed graph. The sets Ȳ_j and P are convex and non-empty.
items.proof_sketch: The graph of a constant correspondence is simply the Cartesian product, which is closed. Non-emptiness and convexity follow from the definitions.
items.context: Verifies Lemma 2.5 conditions for production units and market participant.

items.statement: For each consumption unit i, the set Ā_i(x̄_i) is convex and non-empty for all x̄_i.
items.proof_sketch: A_i(x̄_i) is defined by a linear inequality in x_i, hence convex. The intersection with the convex set C remains convex. By Assumption IV.a, there exists x'_i ∈ X_i with x'_i ≤ ω_i. As shown in 3.1.2, x'_i ∈ A_i(x̄_i) for all x̄_i. Since x'_i ∈ X*_i ⊂ int(C) by construction, x'_i ∈ Ā_i(x̄_i), so Ā_i(x̄_i) is non-empty.
items.context: Verifies the convexity and non-emptiness condition of Lemma 2.5 for consumption units.

items.statement: The graph of Ā_i(x̄_i) is a closed set.
items.proof_sketch: The budget constraint is a weak inequality between two continuous functions of the action profile a, so the graph is closed.
items.context: Verifies the closed graph condition of Lemma 2.5 for consumption units.

items.statement: If p·ω_i > min_{x_i ∈ X̄_i} p·x_i, then Ā_i(x̄_i) is continuous at the point x̄_i = (x_1, …, x_{i−1}, x_{i+1}, …, x_m, y_1, …, y_n, p).
items.proof: Let r_i = p·ω_i + max[0, Σ_j α_{ij} p·y_j]. When x̄^k_i converges to x̄_i, p^k → p and r^k_i → r_i. Consider x_i ∈ Ā_i(x̄_i), so x_i ∈ X̄_i and p·x_i ≤ r_i. Case (a): If p·x_i < r_i, then for k sufficiently large, p^k·x_i < r^k_i, so x^k_i = x_i works. Case (b): If p·x_i = r_i, choose x'_i ∈ X̄_i with p·x'_i < p·ω_i ≤ r_i (exists by hypothesis). Define x_i(λ) = λx_i + (1−λ)x'_i. For λ^k = min[1, (r^k_i − p^k·x'_i)/(p^k·x_i − p^k·x'_i)], we have x_i(λ^k) ∈ Ā_i(x̄^k_i) for all k sufficiently large. Since p·x_i = r_i > p·x'_i, the denominator is positive for large k; and lim r^k_i = r_i = lim p^k·x_i implies lim λ^k = 1, so lim x_i(λ^k) = x_i.
items.context: Formally labeled REMARK with PROOF. Establishes the continuity of the budget correspondence, the most delicate condition of Lemma 2.5.

notation_in_scope.r_i: income = p·ω_i + max[0, Σ_j α_{ij} p·y_j]

items.statement: If Assumption IV.a holds, then the condition p·ω_i > min_{x_i ∈ X̄_i} p·x_i is trivially satisfied for any p ∈ P and y_j ∈ Ȳ_j (j = 1, …, n).
items.proof_sketch: By IV.a, there exists x'_i ∈ X_i with ω_i > x'_i (strict componentwise). Since p ≥ 0 and p ≠ 0, p·ω_i > p·x'_i ≥ min p·x_i.
items.context: Ensures the Remark's condition holds universally under Assumption IV.a.

items.statement: All conditions of Lemma 2.5 are satisfied for the abstract economy Ē, and therefore Ē has an equilibrium point.
items.proof_sketch: Compactness and convexity: Claims 3.3.4_a, 3.3.4_b. Continuity and quasi-concavity of payoffs: Claim 3.3.4_c. Continuity, closed graph, convexity and non-emptiness of constraint correspondences: Claims 3.3.4_d, 3.3.4_e, 3.3.4_f, Remark_3.3.5, Claim_3.3.5_a.
items.context: Establishes existence of equilibrium for the bounded/truncated economy. It remains to show this is also an equilibrium of the original economy E.

items.statement: At an Ē-equilibrium, p*·z* ≤ 0, z*_h ≤ 0 for all h (i.e., z* ≤ 0), and x*_i and y*_j are interior points of C.
items.proof: From Assumption I.a and the definition of C, 0 ∈ Ȳ_j for each j. So as in 3.1.2, max[0, Σ_j α_{ij} p*·ȳ*_j] = Σ_j α_{ij} p*·ȳ*_j. From the budget constraint, p*·x̄*_i ≤ p*·ω_i + Σ_j α_{ij} p*·ȳ*_j. Summing over i and using Σ_i α_{ij} = 1: p*·z* ≤ 0. For fixed z*, p* maximizes p·z* for p ∈ P; by the unit vector argument (as in 3.2), z*_h ≤ 0 for all h. Then x*_i ∈ X*_i and y*_j ∈ Y*_j, which are interior to C by construction.
items.context: The interiority of equilibrium points in C is crucial: it means the truncation does not bind at equilibrium.

items.statement: At an Ē-equilibrium, x*_i maximizes u_i(x_i) subject to x_i ∈ A_i(x̄*_i) (the original, untruncated budget set).
items.proof: Suppose for some x'_i ∈ A_i(x̄*_i), u_i(x'_i) > u_i(x*_i). By Assumption III.c (strict quasi-concavity), u_i(tx'_i + (1−t)x*_i) > u_i(x*_i) for 0 < t < 1. For t sufficiently small, tx'_i + (1−t)x*_i belongs to C (since x*_i is interior to C). Also tx'_i + (1−t)x*_i ∈ A_i(x̄*_i) by convexity of A_i. Hence tx'_i + (1−t)x*_i ∈ Ā_i(x̄*_i), contradicting the fact that x*_i is an Ē equilibrium.
items.context: Equation (2) in 3.4.1. Shows the truncation does not constrain the consumer's optimum.

items.statement: At an Ē-equilibrium, y*_j maximizes p*·y_j subject to y_j ∈ Y_j (the original, untruncated production set).
items.proof: Suppose for some y'_j ∈ Y_j, p*·y'_j > p*·y*_j. Then p*·(ty'_j + (1−t)y*_j) > p*·y*_j for 0 < t < 1. For t sufficiently small, ty'_j + (1−t)y*_j ∈ Ȳ_j (since y*_j is interior to C), contradicting the Ē equilibrium character of y*_j.
items.context: Equation (3) in 3.4.1. Same interior-point argument as for consumers, applied to firms.

items.statement: p* maximizes p·z* for p ∈ P, directly from the definition of equilibrium for Ē, since the domain of p is the same in both abstract economies E and Ē.
The point (x*_1, …, x*_m, y*_1, …, y*_n, p*) is an equilibrium point for E, and therefore a competitive equilibrium. Theorem I has been proved.
items.proof: x*_i maximizes u_i over A_i(x̄*_i) (Claim_3.4.1_b). y*_j maximizes p*·y_j over Y_j (Claim_3.4.1_c). p* maximizes p·z* over P (Claim_3.4.1_d). Hence the point is an E equilibrium. By Claim_3.2_d, it is a competitive equilibrium.
items.context: Concludes the proof of Theorem I (stated in Part 1 of the paper).

items.statement: Assumption IV'.a: ω_i ∈ R^l; for some x_i ∈ X_i, x_i ≤ ω_i, and for at least one h ∈ 𝔓, x_{hi} < ω_{hi}. Here 𝔓 is the set of productive labor types defined in 4.4. IV'.a is a weakening of IV.a: it is now only supposed that the individual is capable of supplying at least one type of productive labor. IV'.a and IV.b together are denoted by IV'.
items.context: Formally stated assumption replacing IV.a.

notation_in_scope.𝔓: set of productive labor types (defined in 4.4)

items.statement: Assumption IV'.a is a weakening of Assumption IV.a.
items.proof_sketch: IV.a requires ω_i > x_i componentwise for some x_i ∈ X_i (a positive amount of every commodity). IV'.a only requires x_i ≤ ω_i with strict inequality for at least one component h ∈ 𝔓.

items.statement: Let X = Σ_{i=1}^m X_i, the Minkowski sum of all consumption sets.

notation_in_scope.X: aggregate consumption set, Minkowski sum of individual consumption sets

items.statement: Assumption V: There exist x ∈ X and y ∈ Y such that x < y + ω (strict componentwise inequality). That is, it is possible to arrange the economic system by choice of production and consumption vectors so that an excess supply of all commodities can be achieved.
items.context: Formally stated assumption for Theorem II.

items.statement: Let 𝔇 be the set of commodities h such that for all i = 1, …, m and all x_i ∈ X_i, if h ∈ 𝔇 then there exists λ > 0 such that x_i + λδ_h ∈ X_i and u_i(x_i + λδ_h) > u_i(x_i). 𝔇 is the set of commodities which are always desired by every consumer.
items.context: Formally labeled DEFINITION. δ_h is the positive unit vector of the hth axis.

items.statement: Assumption VI: The set 𝔇 (of commodities always desired by every consumer) is not empty.
items.context: Formally stated assumption. A stronger form of Assumption III.b.

items.statement: Let 𝔇' be the set of commodities h such that for all i = 1, …, m and all x_i ∈ X̂_i (the set of consumption vectors compatible with existing resource and technological conditions), if h ∈ 𝔇' then there exists λ > 0 such that x_i + λδ_h ∈ X_i and u_i(x_i + λδ_h) > u_i(x_i).
items.context: Formally labeled DEFINITION. Weakened version of 𝔇 restricted to feasible consumption vectors.

notation_in_scope.𝔇': set of desired commodities (weakened, restricted to feasible consumption)
notation_in_scope.X̂_i: set of consumption vectors compatible with resource and technology constraints

items.statement: Assumption VI': The set 𝔇' is not empty.
items.context: Formally stated. VI can be weakened to VI'.

items.statement: Let 𝔓 be the set of commodities h such that: (a) if y ∈ Y, then y_h ≤ 0 (commodity h cannot be produced — it is a type of labor), and (b) for any y ∈ Y, there exists y' ∈ Y such that for all h' ≠ h, y'_{h'} ≥ y_{h'}, while for at least one h'' ∈ 𝔇, y'_{h''} > y_{h''} (increasing the input of labor type h can increase the output of at least one desired commodity without decreasing any other commodity).
items.context: Formally labeled DEFINITION. 𝔓 consists of types of labor that are always productive. Part (a): labor cannot be produced. Part (b): additional labor of type h can always increase output of some desired commodity.

items.statement: Assumption VII: The set 𝔓 (of productive labor types) is not empty.
items.context: Formally stated. Rules out situations of limitational factors in which the marginal productivity of all types of labor (in terms of desired commodities) is zero.

items.statement: In conjunction with IV'.a and VI, Assumption VII ensures that any individual possesses the ability to supply a commodity which has at least derived value.
items.proof_sketch: IV'.a guarantees each consumer can supply some labor h ∈ 𝔓. VII guarantees that h is productive (can increase output of some h'' ∈ 𝔇). VI guarantees h'' is desired. Together: each consumer can contribute something of derived value.
items.context: Explains why all three assumptions are needed in combination.

items.statement: Assumption VII is satisfied if there is a productive process turning a form of labor into a desired commodity without the need of complementary commodities (e.g., domestic service or personal services).
items.proof_sketch: If labor type h can directly produce a desired commodity h'' ∈ 𝔇 without complementary inputs, then condition (b) of the definition of 𝔓 is satisfied.
items.context: Provides a sufficient condition for VII to hold.

items.statement: A case where Assumption VII might not hold is an economic system with fixed technological coefficients where production requiring a given type of labor also requires, directly or indirectly, some complementary factors. In this case, equilibrium may be impossible: for any positive level of real wages, labor supply may exceed the maximum employable quantity; at zero wages, demand is positive but labor supply is zero. The discontinuity of the labor supply curve as real wages go to zero prevents equilibrium.
items.proof_sketch: With fixed coefficients and complementary resource limitations, there is a maximum employable labor quantity. Labor supply is relatively inelastic and may not vanish as wages approach zero (poverty effect). This creates a discontinuity preventing market clearing.
items.context: Heuristic argument for why Assumption VII is necessary, corresponding to structural unemployment.

items.statement: Let Ŷ = { y | y ∈ Y, there exist x_i ∈ X_i for all i such that z ≤ 0 }. Ŷ is the set of aggregate production vectors compatible with feasible consumption.
items.context: Introduced for the weakened version VII' of Assumption VII.

items.statement: Let 𝔓' be the set of commodities h such that: (a) if y ∈ Y, then y_h ≤ 0, and (b) if y ∈ Ŷ, then for some y' ∈ Y and all h' ≠ h, y'_{h'} ≥ y_{h'}, while for at least one h'' ∈ 𝔇, y'_{h''} > y_{h''}.
items.context: Formally labeled DEFINITION. Weakened version of 𝔓 restricted to feasible production vectors.

notation_in_scope.𝔓': weakened set of productive labor types

items.statement: Assumption VII': The set 𝔓' is not empty.
items.context: VII can be weakened to VII'.

items.statement: Assumptions III.b, VI, and VII can simultaneously be weakened to III'.b, VI', and VII' respectively.
For an economic system satisfying Assumptions I–III, IV' (i.e., IV'.a and IV.b), and V–VII, there is a competitive equilibrium.
items.proof_sketch: The proof (Section 5) proceeds similarly to Theorem I. Define P_ε = { p ∈ P : p_h ≥ ε for all h ∈ 𝔓 }. Consider the modified abstract economy E^ε with price domain P_ε. Show E^ε has an equilibrium for each ε > 0 (using the same compactification technique as Theorem I, with the Remark in 3.3.5 applicable via condition (1) of 5.0). Then show that for some ε, the E^ε equilibrium is also an E equilibrium.
items.context: Formally labeled THEOREM II. The main result generalizing Theorem I to weaker endowment assumptions.

items.statement: Let π be the number of elements of 𝔓. For any ε with 0 < ε < π, define P_ε = { p | p ∈ P, p_h ≥ ε for all h ∈ 𝔓 }.
items.context: P_ε contracts the price domain to ensure productive labor types have strictly positive prices.

notation_in_scope.P_ε: restricted price simplex with p_h ≥ ε for h ∈ 𝔓

items.statement: For any p ∈ P_ε, there exists x_i ∈ X_i such that p·x_i < p·ω_i. That is, the budget constraint is strictly satisfiable for all prices in P_ε.
items.proof: From IV'.a, choose x_i ∈ X_i so that x_{hi} ≤ ω_{hi} for all h and x_{h'i} < ω_{h'i} for some h' ∈ 𝔓. For any p ∈ P_ε, p·(ω_i − x_i) = Σ_h p_h(ω_{hi} − x_{hi}) ≥ p_{h'}(ω_{h'i} − x_{h'i}) > 0 since p_{h'} ≥ ε > 0 and ω_{h'i} − x_{h'i} > 0. Hence p·x_i < p·ω_i.
items.context: Equation (1) of 5.0. This is the crucial property that P_ε provides: the cheaper-point condition, enabling the continuity argument of Remark 3.3.5. This property may fail for general p ∈ P under IV'.a.

items.statement: Define the abstract economy E^ε = [X_1, …, X_m, Y_1, …, Y_n, P_ε, u_1(x_1), …, u_m(x_m), p·y_1, …, p·y_n, p·z, A_1(x̄_1), …, A_m(x̄_m), Y_1, …, Y_n, P_ε]. E^ε is the same as E except that the price domain has been contracted from P to P_ε.
items.context: The proof strategy for Theorem II: first show E^ε has an equilibrium for each ε, then show some E^ε equilibrium is also an E equilibrium.

notation_in_scope.E^ε: abstract economy with restricted price domain P_ε

items.statement: The existence of an equilibrium point for E^ε for each ε > 0 can be shown by the same compactification technique as in the proof of Theorem I (intersecting action domains with a suitable hypercube and applying Lemma 2.5). The Remark of 3.3.5 is applicable because Claim_5.0_a ensures p·ω_i > min p·x_i for all p ∈ P_ε.
items.proof_sketch: The same boundedness arguments (3.3.1–3.3.2) apply. The Remark of 3.3.5 is applicable because Claim_5.0_a ensures the cheaper-point condition holds for all p ∈ P_ε.
items.context: The introduction of P_ε is necessitated by the fact that condition (1) of 5.0 may not hold for all p ∈ P, and the Remark's condition in 3.3.5 may not be satisfied for all p ∈ P under the weaker Assumption IV'.a.

items.statement: At an equilibrium point of E^ε (if it exists), p*·z* ≤ 0.
items.proof: Since x*_i ∈ A_i(x̄*_i), p*·x*_i ≤ p*·ω_i + Σ_j α_{ij} p*·y*_j (see also 3.1.2). Summing over i and using Σ_i α_{ij} = 1: p*·(Σ_i x*_i − Σ_j y*_j − ω) ≤ 0, i.e., p*·z* ≤ 0.
items.context: This section is described as 'purely heuristic, designed to motivate the choice of the hypercube.' The inequality p*·z* ≤ 0 is Walras' inequality (not equality, since the weakened assumptions may not give equality at this stage).

notation_in_scope.z*: excess demand at equilibrium of E^ε
